prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, bringing optical frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (B012) as a single two-person part. Having read all eight first-round statements and the chair's questions, my reasoning is unchanged on the science and sharper on the wording. Katori's magic-wavelength condition lets the trap perturb both clock levels equally, so thousands of atoms are held free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and Ye's group converted that into the 10^-18 regime with ultrastable lasers and systematic control. The performance is confirmed in independent laboratories, clock-to-clock comparisons across institutes are routine, and it already supports millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, constraints on varying constants and relativistic geodesy. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb, not this architecture. I have not changed my configuration since round 1 (B012 alone, with B022 now as first alternative and B038 second); what has changed is that four members hold B022 and four hold B012 and each side names the other as its alternative, so the decision is really about whether maturity and clean attribution outweigh breadth. I think they do this year, though narrowly, and I would accept B022 if the credit questions are resolved.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Trapped-ion clocks, SYRTE, PTB, NIST and other lattice-clock groups, and the JILA team members, all contributed to the 10^-18 milestone, and priority for the magic-wavelength idea over contemporaneous proposals has still not been checked by this committee. A Katori-Ye pair draws a line some will contest, which is why the citation should be built around the lattice-clock architecture and not record numbers or clocks in general. The B012 case is also an instrument-level result rather than a new phenomenon, the SI second has not yet been redefined, and Danielsson and Mehlig weigh breadth and new physics more heavily than I do. On B022 the other side of the ledger is real: the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 observations is the best theory-to-experiment narrative on the list, and I may be underweighting a very large new field.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the unresolved superconducting mechanism in B022 is an interpretation question separate from a secure discovery, that prizes have honoured results before their microscopic explanation, and that a new regime of matter outweighs clean attribution on an instrument.
responses.response: I accept the logical separation: correlated insulators and superconducting domes near the magic angle are reproduced widely, and I no longer think the open pairing mechanism alone disqualifies B022. My remaining concern is narrower and about the discovery itself, namely sample-to-sample twist-angle disorder and how many of the correlated states are understood well enough to be named in a citation, which makes it harder to write a short sentence that will stay correct. On scope I disagree with a hierarchy that puts new phenomena above new measurement capability; a 10^-18 clock changes what can be tested, which is a discovery of the same kind. If your citation stays strictly at the flat-band prediction and observed phases, the maturity gap shrinks, and that is the reason B022 is my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson cautions that the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gives flat bands but does not predict the correlated phases, so the B022 citation must not suggest that theory predicted the superconductivity, and he concedes that waiting would settle interpretation and credit.
responses.response: This is the point that moves my view of B022 most. If the theory credit is limited to the flat-band prediction, then the neat prediction-then-discovery story is weaker than the chair's summary suggests, because the part of the experiment that made the field, the correlated and superconducting states, was not predicted by the three-name theory side. Your own concession that waiting would clarify both interpretation and credit is, to me, an argument for B012 now and B022 in a later year when the authorship and attribution record is clearer. I would not ask you to give up B022; I ask whether, on your own wording, the prediction and the observation are still one achievement or two.

responses.point: Kroll wants the B012 citation worded around the lattice-clock architecture and its 10^-18 realisation so that ion-clock and comb contributors are not implicitly demoted, and treats the pending SI redefinition as supporting evidence and not a criterion.
responses.response: I agree and have drafted the citation accordingly, naming the optical lattice clock with many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, with 10^-18 mentioned as the milestone and not as a record. I accept your treatment of the SI second: in round 1 I asked whether it had to happen first, and I now think it should not, since the redefinition follows from the demonstrated performance and independent comparisons, not the other way round. Where I remain cautious, as you are, is priority; I cannot verify from the supplied material that Katori's proposal precedes contemporaneous magic-wavelength proposals, and I would want that recorded as a reservation and not assumed.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, asks that the author record of the first B022 reports be examined before final votes and holds that the credit gap exists for nearly every candidate and is not disqualifying; he also says B012 is the strongest alternative and he would support it if the moire field is judged too young.
responses.response: I take the first request seriously, and in fact it works against B022 in my reading: if the first author and Dean's group have to be weighed against a three-name cap, the committee is no longer comparing a clean allocation with a clean allocation. Your statement that the credit gap is common to most candidates is fair in general, but the B012 gap is limited to adjacent groups, while the B022 gap includes the person who ran the 2018 measurements. I also note that you would support B012 on a maturity judgment, and my judgment is that eight years with an open mechanism and variable samples is, on balance, early. On your question of a two-part prize, I have also not found a split of three names that is fair to both sets and I would not recommend one.

responses.point: Mehlig regards the unresolved pairing mechanism as separate from the discovery, calls the supplied B022 theory credit defensible because the Bistritzer-MacDonald model identified the magic angle quantitatively in a form experiments could target, and accepts that other theory groups worked on flat bands.
responses.response: I agree that the model located the angle quantitatively and that the experiments targeted it, and this is a genuine strength that I weigh more than I did in my opening ranking. We still differ on how to read the evidence of reproducibility: you see it as the decisive point, while I see reproduction across eight years as less than the independent confirmation and cross-institute comparison that B012 has had for longer. I do not expect to persuade you, and I want to be clear that I would find a B022 prize with a narrow citation acceptable if the committee's credit review is satisfactory.

responses.point: Lindroth separates the prize question from metrology administration, wants the citation to cite the broader clock community in its wording without adding names, and notes that B038 attribution mixes two routes (BB84 and Ekert's entanglement-based protocol).
responses.response: I agree with you on the first two points, and I now treat the pending redefinition as irrelevant to whether the discovery is mature. On B038, you were right that Bennett-Brassard and Ekert are two separate routes that a three-name citation would have to unify, and with the duplicate Ekert spelling and Wiesner's earlier conjugate coding unresolved I am not pressing it. I list B038 as an alternative only as a record of my opening view, not as something I would vote for this year.

uncertainties: Whether priority for the magic-wavelength proposal over contemporaneous proposals holds; I cannot verify it from the supplied material.

Whether the committee treats a precision-measurement invention as a prize-level discovery of the same kind as a new regime of quantum matter; Danielsson and Mehlig do not, and that disagreement is not resolvable by evidence.
Whether the B022 credit for the first experimental reports can be fixed within three names, and whether the open mechanism and sample variability will matter in a few years.
Whether my own closeness to quantum-technology programmes affects how I weigh a metrology invention against moire matter; I cannot judge that bias fully.
statement.conflict_note: I am a Chalmers professor and director of WACQT, a quantum-computing programme, with documented Chalmers links to the 2025 laureates and a collaborator network in superconducting circuits. None of B012, B022 or B038 involves a documented personal or institutional connection to me, and I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Bennett, Brassard or Ekert. I note that the chair's summary records my declared bias toward quantum information as a possible effect, which is why I do not rely on B038 and have not preferred a circuit-QED or quantum-computing candidate. I see no need for recusal on any shortlisted part.
